title: Where children once began
hookLine: Jewish children traditionally started Torah with Leviticus: let the pure come and study purity (Leviticus Rabbah 7:3)

cards: Pick the first Bible story for a five-year-old, and you'd probably reach for Genesis: light and darkness, animals two by two, a rainbow. For many centuries, in many Jewish communities, that's not what happened.
A small child came to school for the first time, sometimes wrapped in a prayer shawl, sometimes given honey on the letters of the alphabet.
Then the teacher opened the Torah, skipped Genesis and Exodus, and began with Leviticus: the book of offerings and priests, the one adults often skip.

teach.b: Why Leviticus? The midrash Leviticus Rabbah asks exactly that. Rabbi Assi says: why do young children begin with the book of the priests and not with Genesis?

teach.h: LET THE PURE STUDY THE PURE.
teach.b: Because the offerings are pure, and the children are pure. Let the pure come and busy themselves with what is pure.
So the book that sounds most distant to adults, all altars and rules of clean and unclean, goes first to the cleanest hands. The rabbis called it Torat Kohanim, the instruction of the priests.

Its Hebrew name, like every book of the Torah's, comes from an early word, here the very first: vayikra, and He called. "And the LORD called unto Moses, and spoke unto him out of the tent of meeting, saying."
Remember where Exodus left Moses: outside the tent, unable to go in, because the cloud filled it. Leviticus opens with God calling him in.

In the weeks ahead, this book brings offerings and their meanings, the priests' first day, and what was clean and unclean. It also holds a chapter on holiness with the line "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."

teach.h: THE BOOK AT THE CENTER: HOLINESS.
teach.b: Leviticus sits at the center of the five books, and its subject is holiness: how ordinary people, with ordinary food and bodies and neighbors, can live close to God.
Children were taught to start there, and so does this path.

how: In many traditional communities, a child's first day of Torah study began with Leviticus, often with honey placed on the letters so learning would taste sweet; the custom of honey is still kept in some schools today.

games.q: you're a teacher in an old Jewish school. a five-year-old has just arrived for the first day of Torah. where do you open the scroll?
o: Genesis: the creation of the world.
games.why: Leviticus. the midrash says: the offerings are pure and the children are pure, so let the pure come and study what is pure.

practice: Open a Bible to Leviticus, chapter one, verse one, or simply hear it again: and the Lord called unto Moses, and spoke unto him out of the tent of meeting.
Read it slowly, the way a child reads a first line, one word at a time, and stay with its first word, called. What's calling you in, these days?

wordCard.voice: Vayikra. And He called. The first word of Leviticus, the book where, for centuries, Jewish children began.
